sections.text:
Jacob, peace be upon him, is a noble prophet, the son of a noble prophet (Isaac), the grandson of a great prophet (Abraham), and the father of a noble prophet (Joseph). He is, as it was said: “The Noble One, the son of the Noble One, the son of the Noble One, the son of the Noble One.”

Jacob is also known as "Israel", which means the servant of God or the elite of God, and to him are attributed the children of Israel with all their twelve tribes (tribes).

Jacob grew up in the house of prophecy and faith, and imbibed wisdom and piety from his childhood in the land of Palestine.

God blessed him with twelve sons, who were physically strong and built, but Jacob had a special love in his heart for his son Joseph and for his younger brother Benjamin.

This special love aroused jealousy and envy in the hearts of Joseph's brothers, so they hatched a plot to get rid of him and keep him away from their father.

They asked their father to take Joseph with them to graze under the pretext of playing, and despite Jacob’s anxiety and fear that the wolf would eat him while they were unaware of him, he agreed after their insistence.

The brothers carried out their plan and threw Joseph into the pit (the dark well), and returned to their father in the evening crying artificially, carrying Joseph’s shirt stained with false blood (sheep blood).

When Jacob saw the shirt intact and not torn, he realized with his wisdom and prophecy that the wolf had not eaten his son, and that they had planned something in secret.

But he did not get angry with insults or revenge. Rather, he responded to this major calamity with the morals of the prophets, and said his immortal sentence: “So patience is beautiful, and God is the one who seeks help in what you describe.”

Many years passed, and the brothers grew up and got married, and Jacob continued to remember Joseph and cry over his separation until his eyes turned white and he lost his sight from extreme sadness and sorrow.

His children were blaming him for crying a lot and remembering Joseph, thinking that he had died and his memory had faded away.

Jacob would respond to them with the certainty of a believer who does not despair of God’s mercy: “I only complain of my grief and my grief to God, and I know from God what you do not know.”

When famine occurred in the Levant, Jacob sent his sons to Egypt to bring food from the dear of Egypt (who was Joseph without them knowing).

On the second trip, Joseph tricked his brother Benjamin into staying with him.

The brothers returned and told their father what had happened to Benjamin and to their older brother, who refused to return out of shame, so Jacob's old and new sorrows were renewed.

Despite this accumulated affliction, his certainty of God’s relief increased, and he ordered his sons to return to search for Joseph and Benjamin, saying: “And do not despair of the Spirit of God. Indeed, none despair of the Spirit of God except the disbelieving people.”

The brothers went to Egypt, where Joseph revealed his true identity to them and forgave them for what they had done.

Joseph gave them his shirt and ordered them to throw it on his father's face to restore his sight.

As soon as the caravan left Egypt heading to the Levant, Jacob said to those around him weeks before the shirt arrived: “Indeed, I smell the scent of Joseph, had you not refuted it.”

Al-Bashir arrived and threw the shirt on Yaqoub’s face, and he immediately recovered, thanks to God!
Jacob became indescribably happy, prostrated to God in thanks, and said to his sons: “Did I not tell you that I know better than God what you do not know?”

Jacob asked forgiveness for his sons and asked God for their forgiveness, and the whole family headed to Egypt and settled there in dignity and glory.

The lesson of Jacob's story is that beautiful patience without complaining to people is the key to relief, and that trusting in God and having good thoughts in Him brings miracles even after long years of pain.
